mcqs.question: In the O(n²) LIS recurrence, dp[i] is computed as max(dp[j] + 1) over which indices j?
options: Every j from 0 to i-1, unconditionally
Only j = i-1, since chains can only extend from the immediately preceding index
Every j from i+1 to n-1 where nums[j] > nums[i]
Every j < i where nums[j] < nums[i]
mcqs.explanation: Only earlier indices with a strictly smaller value can validly extend into an increasing chain ending at i — extending from an equal or larger value would break the strictly-increasing requirement, and extending from an unconditional earlier index would ignore the value constraint entirely.

mcqs.question: Why is 'dp[i] = LIS length using the first i elements' a different, incompatible definition from the one this topic uses?
options: It's actually the same definition, just phrased differently
It gives a running maximum that never needs to check whether a chain can extend from a specific earlier index, so it can't produce the recurrence dp[i] = max(dp[j]+1 for valid j)
It only works for arrays with no duplicate values
It requires an extra O(n) pass to compute correctly
mcqs.explanation: These are genuinely different definitions: 'ending exactly at i' lets the recurrence ask 'can nums[i] extend a chain that stopped at j,' which needs to know precisely where a chain terminates. 'Using the first i elements' collapses that information into a running max and can't support the extension check at all.

mcqs.question: In the patience-sorting approach, why does tails[k] track the smallest tail value for chains of length k+1, rather than any tail value?
options: Because the smallest tail is always part of the true optimal subsequence
Tracking any tail would use less memory
A smaller tail value is at least as extensible as a larger one for the same chain length, so keeping the smallest strictly dominates and lets every other chain of that length be safely discarded
Because the array must stay sorted for the algorithm to terminate
mcqs.explanation: Any future element that could extend a chain ending in a larger value can also extend a chain of the same length ending in a smaller one, so the smaller tail is never worse and often better — that's what justifies discarding every other chain of that length.

mcqs.question: After running the O(n log n) patience-sorting LIS algorithm, can you read the final tails array as the actual longest increasing subsequence?
options: Yes, tails always equals a valid LIS of the input
No — only its length is meaningful; its contents get overwritten by later values and generally aren't a subsequence that appeared together in the input
Yes, but only if the input has no duplicate values
No — the length is also wrong, only the DP version gives a correct length
mcqs.explanation: tails only tracks the smallest achievable tail per chain length, and its entries get overwritten by unrelated later elements — its length matches the LIS length, but its contents don't reconstruct an actual valid subsequence. Recovering the real chain needs the O(n²) DP's prev-pointer approach.

mcqs.question: To adapt the patience-sorting LIS to allow non-decreasing (rather than strictly increasing) chains, what changes?
options: The whole algorithm must switch back to the O(n²) DP version
Use bisect_right instead of bisect_left when searching tails, so equal values extend an existing chain instead of replacing a tail
Sort the input array first
Nothing changes — the same code already handles both cases identically
mcqs.explanation: Switching the binary search from bisect_left to bisect_right changes how equal values are placed: they now extend the rightmost matching chain rather than being treated as a stricter replacement, which is exactly the behavior non-decreasing sequences need. No algorithmic downgrade is required.
